lessons.title: Stock car, not stock
lessons.objective: Explain why a stock car is not a showroom car.

payload.prompt: Which one is the race car?

image.alt: Two cars side by side: left is a street Camry with headlights and bumpers; right is a NASCAR stock car with no headlights, simplified body, and racing slicks.

options.text: The street car on the left
The stock car on the right

cues: Look for slick racing tires, no headlights, and a simplified body.

explanation.correct: Right. The stock car has purpose-built parts even though it looks like a showroom model.
explanation.incorrect: The stock car is the one with racing slicks, no street lights, and a reinforced cage. It is built to a strict rulebook, not sold in showrooms.

payload.prompt: Why are stock cars called 'stock' if they are not street cars?

options.text: They use old parts left over from past years.
Their bodies resemble showroom models but are purpose-built to a strict rulebook.
They are mass-produced on the same line as regular cars.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The name is about the bodyline styling, not the parts inside.
explanation.incorrect: Stock cars are called 'stock' because their outer shapes resemble showroom models, but every part inside is built to NASCAR spec and purpose-built for racing.

payload.prompt: Match the car part to its role.

pairs.definition: The frame that holds the car together and carries the load.
Lightweight panels that give the car its showroom-like shape.
A steel structure that protects the driver if the car flips.
Foam-filled wall outside the track that absorbs impact.

distractorDefinitions: A painted layer that makes the car look faster.
A device that limits fuel consumption.

explanation.summary: Stock cars are built with a steel frame, lightweight panels, and layers of safety tech.

payload.prompt: Stock cars are built to {{regulation}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Every car must meet the same spec for fairness.
explanation.incorrect: Stock cars follow a strict rulebook: same engine size, body shape limits, fuel tank capacity. Parity is the goal.

payload.prompt: Are NASCAR chassis made of aluminum to save weight?

scene.alt: Overhead view of a chassis frame in the shop, tubes clearly visible.

choices.label: No, steel tube handles impact best.

explanation.correct: Right. Steel handles the repeated stress and crashes better than aluminum.
explanation.incorrect: NASCAR chassis are steel-tube frames, not aluminum. Steel is stiffer and safer for impacts at 180+ mph.

lessons.title: The Next Gen car
lessons.objective: Name what changed with the Next Gen car.

payload.prompt: When did the Next Gen car first race in Cup?

explanation.correct: Exactly. The Next Gen car premiered in 2022 and is still in use in 2026.
explanation.incorrect: The Next Gen car started in 2022. It replaced the old Gen 6 car and introduced symmetry, independent rear suspension, and single-lug wheels.

payload.prompt: Tap the independent rear suspension.

diagram.alt: Side profile of a Next Gen car showing symmetrical body, independent rear suspension arms, and single-lug center-lock wheel.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The independent rear suspension lets each rear wheel move independently.
explanation.incorrect: The independent rear suspension is a rear-suspension system where each wheel can move independently from the other.

payload.prompt: Match the Next Gen change to what it does.

pairs.definition: Left and right sides are identical, reducing part inventory and cost.
Each rear wheel moves on its own, improving handling over bumps.
One center-lock nut per wheel instead of five, but trickier pit stops.
Lightweight panels shared across all three brands for cost control.

distractorDefinitions: A new engine with more horsepower.
A special fuel blend for better mileage.

explanation.summary: Next Gen prioritized shared parts, cost control, and safety while keeping racing competitive.

payload.statement: The single-lug wheel cost us the race.

options.text: One center-lock nut per wheel made a pit stop slow or the wheel stuck.
The wheel was cheap and fell off.
The engine is not compatible with single wheels.

payload.translation: The pit crew had trouble with the single-lug wheel nut during the stop.
followUps: A single center-lock lug (2022+) replaces five traditional lug nuts, making stops faster in theory but trickier if the nut jams.
Next Gen wheel changes make pit stops a different skill compared to Gen 6 (2014-2021).
payload.noFakeExpertNote: This is experienced crew talk; fans usually hear about it after a lost race.

payload.prompt: Does the symmetrical body mean every car looks exactly the same?

scene.alt: Factory photo of multiple Next Gen cars with identical body shapes but different paint schemes.

choices.label: No, the body shape is the same but paint and sponsors differ.
Yes, every car must be identical.

explanation.correct: Right. Symmetry means the left and right shapes are the same, but teams paint them differently.
explanation.incorrect: Symmetry means the chassis and body molds are identical left-to-right, but paint schemes and sponsor logos make each car unique.

lessons.title: Engines and horsepower
lessons.objective: Explain why horsepower differs by track.

payload.prompt: In 2026, how many horsepower do Cup cars make at superspeedways?

explanation.correct: Close. About 510 hp at Daytona and Talladega, limited by a 7-inch tapered spacer.
explanation.incorrect: Superspeedways (Daytona, Talladega, Atlanta) use about 510 hp with a small spacer to prevent runaway speeds in pack racing.

payload.prompt: What does the tapered spacer on top of the engine do?

options.text: Limits the air entering the engine, which reduces horsepower.
Improves aerodynamics by reducing drag.
Cools the engine faster on hot days.

explanation.correct: Exactly. A smaller spacer opening means less air and less power.
explanation.incorrect: The tapered spacer sits on the intake manifold and restricts airflow. A 7-inch spacer at superspeedways limits power; an 8-inch (or larger) at short tracks allows more.

payload.prompt: All Cup engines are naturally aspirated {{size}} V8s.
payload.template: All Cup engines are naturally aspirated {{size}} V8s.

explanation.correct: Right. 358 ci is the spec for all three manufacturers in 2026.
explanation.incorrect: Every Cup car uses the same 358 cubic-inch V8 engine, naturally aspirated. Power varies by track via the tapered spacer, not by engine size.

payload.prompt: Which engine is a V8?

image.alt: Two engine diagrams: left shows four cylinders in a line (inline-4); right shows eight cylinders in a V shape (V8).

options.text: The inline engine on the left
The V8 on the right

cues: Count the cylinders and look for the V shape.

explanation.correct: Right. A V8 has eight cylinders arranged in two banks of four.
explanation.incorrect: The V8 has eight cylinders in a V configuration. The inline engine on the left is simpler but lower power.

facts.label: Driver feedback
facts.value: Too loose on exit, hard to control.

options.text: Keep the 8-inch spacer; setup and tires handle the power.
options.consequence: The driver learns to manage the horsepower. 750 hp at Bristol is the 2026 spec.
options.considerations: Horsepower is not the issue; balance and tire pressure are.

options.text: Request a smaller spacer for less power.
options.consequence: NASCAR does not allow spacer changes during the weekend.
options.considerations: The spacer is fixed by the rules and track type. You solve a loose car with adjustments, not engine power.

options.text: Switch to a leaner fuel mixture for smoother power delivery.
options.consequence: Helps a bit but not the core issue; the 750 hp is manageable with the right setup.
options.considerations: Fuel mapping helps, but the real fix is chassis balance and tire pressures.

payload.expertNote: Short tracks with high horsepower require precision setup, not less power.
payload.safetyNote: High horsepower at short, tight tracks demands respect and good setup.

lessons.title: Three brands
lessons.objective: Spot Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota nose cues.

payload.prompt: Which one is the Chevrolet nose?

image.alt: Three NASCAR nose designs: Chevy with angular pointed shape, Ford with rounded smooth shape, Toyota with tall vertical grille.

options.text: The pointed nose on the left
The rounded nose in the middle
The tall nose on the right

cues: Chevy has an angular, pointed splitter shape.
Toyota is taller with a vertical profile.

explanation.correct: Right. Chevy's nose is angular and pointed. Ford is smooth; Toyota is tall.
explanation.incorrect: Each brand has distinct nose shapes even though the overall body is symmetrical. Learn the splitter and grille shape to spot them at a glance.

payload.prompt: Match the brand to its nose or identity cue.

pairs.definition: Angular, pointed splitter and nose shape; bowtie logo heritage.
Smooth, rounded splitter and aerodynamic front; oval logo.
Taller nose with vertical grille; three-oval logo.

distractorDefinitions: All three brands use identical body shapes.
The engine determines the brand, not the nose.

explanation.summary: Spotting brands by nose shape is key to following pit strategies and team rivalries.

payload.prompt: Why does brand matter in NASCAR?

options.text: Each brand sponsors different drivers and has fan loyalty.
Different brands have different engine sizes.
One brand is always faster.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Fans are Ford, Chevy or Toyota loyalists, and sponsors tie to manufacturers.
explanation.incorrect: All three brands use the same 358 ci engine and follow the same rules. Brand is about factory support, sponsors and fan identity.

options.text: She is a loyal Ford fan, following Ford-badged teams and drivers.
She works for the Ford company.
Ford cars are faster than Chevy in racing.

payload.translation: She follows Ford-badged NASCAR teams and drivers.
followUps: Ford fans might support teams like Penske, which run Ford engines, or individual drivers who race for Ford.
Manufacturer loyalty is as strong in NASCAR as team loyalty, rooted in factory support and heritage.
payload.noFakeExpertNote: Brand loyalty runs deep in the NASCAR family.

payload.prompt: Is one manufacturer guaranteed to be faster?

scene.alt: Pit box with three cars: one Chevy, one Ford, one Toyota, all with similar looking pit crews and equipment.

choices.label: No, they all follow the same rules and specs.

explanation.correct: Right. All three brands use the same engine, tires and body. Speed comes from the team, not the brand.
explanation.incorrect: Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota all follow identical rules. Speed differences come from team engineering, driver skill and setup, not brand.

lessons.title: Wings and lips
lessons.objective: Explain what a spoiler and splitter do.

payload.prompt: Tap the rear spoiler.

diagram.alt: Side view of a NASCAR car showing rear wing/spoiler standing tall, and front bumper with splitter lip.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The rear spoiler is the tall vertical wing adding downforce and drag.
explanation.incorrect: The rear spoiler is the tall wing at the back. The front splitter is the lip under the nose that keeps air from flowing under the car.

payload.prompt: What does a taller rear spoiler do?

options.text: Adds downforce and drag, slowing the car but improving grip.
Reduces drag and makes the car faster.
Only affects the car's appearance, not performance.

explanation.correct: Right. Downforce improves handling but costs top-end speed due to drag.
explanation.incorrect: A taller spoiler increases downforce (keeps the car glued to the track) but also increases aerodynamic drag (slows it down). Teams balance these effects by track.

payload.prompt: How much speed does a tall spoiler cost in top-end mph?

explanation.correct: Close. A tall spoiler can cost 5-10 mph on a superspeedway.
explanation.incorrect: Aero drag from a taller spoiler costs roughly 5-10 mph depending on the track. Teams use taller spoilers at tracks where downforce matters more than top speed.

payload.prompt: The front splitter keeps air from flowing {{direction}} the car.
payload.template: The front splitter keeps air from flowing {{direction}} the car.

explanation.correct: Right. The splitter blocks air from going under the nose, creating a pressure zone that adds downforce.
explanation.incorrect: The splitter is a lip under the front bumper that prevents air from flowing underneath the car, which increases downforce and grip.

payload.prompt: Do superspeedways like Daytona use taller spoilers than short tracks?

scene.alt: Two cars side by side: Daytona car with low spoiler; Bristol car with tall spoiler.

choices.label: No, Daytona uses a lower spoiler for less drag.
Yes, all tracks use the same spoiler size.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Superspeedways need lower drag, so they use a shorter spoiler.
explanation.incorrect: Superspeedways (Daytona, Talladega) use a lower spoiler to reduce drag and preserve top speed. Short tracks use taller spoilers for better handling grip.

lessons.title: Tires and fuel
lessons.objective: Explain what Goodyear tires and E15 fuel mean for racing.

payload.prompt: All NASCAR Cup cars use {{brand}} slick racing tires.
payload.template: All NASCAR Cup cars use {{brand}} slick racing tires.

explanation.correct: Right. Goodyear is NASCAR's sole tire supplier.
explanation.incorrect: Goodyear is the exclusive tire supplier to Cup Series. Teams cannot choose other brands; they all use Goodyear slicks.

payload.prompt: What is E15 fuel in NASCAR?

options.text: Fuel with 15% ethanol blended in.
A high-octane racing fuel that is illegal for street cars.
Fuel that burns at exactly 15% efficiency.

explanation.correct: Exactly. E15 is regular gasoline with 15% ethanol, the same blend sold at many street pumps.
explanation.incorrect: E15 is a fuel blend: 85% gasoline and 15% ethanol. It is also sold at public gas stations in the US, so it is not exotic fuel.

payload.prompt: Match the tire term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A racing tire with no tread, used on dry tracks for maximum grip.
A rubber mixture designed for high-speed friction and wear.
Speed lost as tires wear throughout a run.
Single nut per wheel on Next Gen cars (2022+).

distractorDefinitions: A tire for wet conditions with raised grooves.
A pit crew member who changes tires.

explanation.summary: Racing tires, falloff and changing methods define pit strategy and race dynamics.

payload.prompt: How many gallons does a NASCAR fuel cell hold?

explanation.correct: Close. The fuel cell holds about 20 gallons in 2026.
explanation.incorrect: A Cup car fuel cell holds approximately 20 gallons. Track length and fuel mileage determine pit strategy.

payload.prompt: Do racing slicks last the entire race without replacement?

scene.alt: Pit stop scene with crew members swapping black Goodyear slick tires.

choices.label: No, teams pit to change worn tires for fresh ones.
Yes, one set of tires lasts the whole race.

explanation.correct: Right. Tires wear, lose grip and are changed during pit stops.
explanation.incorrect: Racing slicks degrade over 20-100 laps depending on track. Teams pit multiple times to change tires, balancing tire freshness with track position.

lessons.title: Who does what
lessons.objective: Match crew chief, spotter, driver and pit crew to jobs.

payload.prompt: Match the pit crew member to their job.

pairs.definition: Removes old tires and bolts new ones (two on the crew).
Lifts the rear of the car off the ground.
Inserts and holds the fuel nozzle into the fuel cell.
Runs fresh tires from the stack to the changers.
The five specialists (changers, jack man, fueler, carrier) who enter the pit stall.

distractorDefinitions: A crew member who washes the windshield.
A person who watches from the bleachers.

explanation.summary: Five people over the wall execute a pit stop in under 12 seconds: precision and athleticism at work.

payload.statement: The spotter says 'clear high' over the radio.

options.text: You can move up safely into the high groove; no cars in your way.
The high bank of the track is clear of debris.
The engine is running clearly at high RPM.

payload.translation: The path is clear in the high lane; move up safely.
followUps: Spotters talk constantly about traffic and lane position. 'Clear low', 'three-wide', 'car right' are common calls.
A spotter's job is camera-eye coverage: they see what the driver cannot and call the racing picture in real time.
payload.noFakeExpertNote: Spotter communication is real-time racing strategy.

payload.prompt: What is the crew chief's main job?

options.text: Engineer and strategist on the pit box; decides pit calls and car adjustments.
Tells the driver how fast to drive.
Manages the pit crew's physical fitness.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The crew chief is the lead engineer and calls every pit stop and adjustment decision.
explanation.incorrect: The crew chief is the strategic and engineering leader. They make pit strategy decisions, authorize adjustments and steer the race from the pit box.

payload.prompt: A pit crew has {{number}} members over the wall during a stop.
payload.template: A pit crew has {{number}} members over the wall during a stop.

explanation.correct: Right. Exactly five: two tire changers, jack man, fueler and tire carrier.
explanation.incorrect: Five crew members go over the wall: the two tire changers, the jack man, the fueler and the tire carrier. No more, no less.

facts.label: Current position
facts.value: Third place, five laps from pit window

facts.label: Fuel estimate
facts.value: Tank will last to lap 150 (pit window at 140-145)

facts.label: Tire condition
facts.value: Front left showing blistering; rear tires OK

options.text: Pit for four tires and fuel to fix the front left.
options.consequence: Fresh tires solve the blister. Team gains grip and protection.
options.considerations: Blistering means the tire is overheating; fresh rubber is the answer. Four tires costs time but fixes the problem.

options.text: Pit for two tires (rear) and fuel to save time.
options.consequence: Faster stop, but worn front left tires may continue blistering.
options.considerations: Two tires is quicker but keeps a bad tire on the car. Acceptable if track position is critical.

options.text: Stay out and let the tires cool down.
options.consequence: Blistering gets worse; the tire could fail.
options.considerations: Tire failure at speed is dangerous and ruins the race. Pitting is the only smart move.

payload.expertNote: Tire blistering is a sign of trouble; fresh rubber is the answer.
payload.safetyNote: A failing tire at race speed is a crash risk; address it immediately.

lessons.title: Safety and inspection
lessons.objective: Explain how safety tech and inspection shape the sport.

payload.prompt: What does the HANS device do?

options.text: Keeps the driver's head and neck stable during sudden impacts.
Monitors the engine temperature.
Adjusts brake pressure during a crash.

explanation.correct: Right. The HANS (Head and Neck Support) prevents whiplash injury.
explanation.incorrect: The HANS device is worn around the driver's neck and shoulders, anchored to the seat. It restrains the head and neck during impacts, preventing whiplash and spinal injury.

facts.label: Race result
facts.value: First place, clear winner, led 200 laps

facts.label: Post-race inspection
facts.value: Car is 0.5 inches too low (violates ride-height rule)

facts.label: Pit crew assessment
facts.value: The car hit the track hard; settling occurred.

options.text: Accept the inspection result; if the car fails, acknowledge and move on.
options.consequence: Integrity is upheld. Penalties (points loss, crew chief suspension) apply if rules were broken.
options.considerations: Inspection is non-negotiable. NASCAR enforces parity and fairness this way.

options.text: Formally appeal the measurement; ask for a recheck.
options.consequence: NASCAR may re-measure. If a mistake happened, appeal works. If the car is genuinely too low, the appeal likely fails.
options.considerations: Appeals are allowed within rules; they must be factual, not emotional.

options.text: Deny any rule breaking and blame the track.
options.consequence: Increased penalties and loss of credibility. NASCAR takes inspection seriously.
options.considerations: Fighting inspection results without evidence hurts the team and the sport.

payload.expertNote: Winning does not exempt a car from inspection. Rules apply equally to the winner and the 40th-place finisher.
payload.safetyNote: Inspection ensures all cars meet the same safety and fairness standards.

payload.prompt: Match the safety feature to its job.

pairs.definition: Steel framework that protects the driver if the car flips or is crushed.
Foam-filled wall outside the track that absorbs impact energy.
Neck and shoulder support that reduces whiplash injury in impacts.
Laminated glass that holds together on impact, protecting the driver.

distractorDefinitions: Padding on the pit box to prevent crew injuries.

explanation.summary: Multiple layers of safety tech protect drivers at extreme speed: cage, barriers, restraints, glass and engineering.

payload.prompt: Is post-race inspection required for every car that finishes?

scene.alt: Garage photo with multiple cars in a line being scanned by inspection equipment.

choices.label: Yes, all cars are inspected for rule compliance.
No, only the winning car is checked.

explanation.correct: Exactly. NASCAR inspects all cars to ensure the field competed on equal terms.
explanation.incorrect: Every car that finishes is subject to post-race inspection. The winner, last place, all of them. Fairness requires equal checking.

payload.prompt: A car that fails inspection may lose {{penalty}}.
payload.template: A car that fails inspection may lose {{penalty}}.

options: only the points from the race

explanation.correct: Right. Inspection failure can cost a win and the points earned.
explanation.incorrect: Post-race inspection failures carry severe penalties: loss of race finish (disqualification), points deduction and crew chief suspension for repeat violations.
